parts.note: base means low, mean or contemptible in character
a ball is the solid shot fired from a cannon or musket

explanation.surface: A golfer or cricketer hits a low, scuffed stroke during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low shot' reads as one stroke in a game, but splits into two separate synonyms, with 'in' only joining them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the American bat-and-ball sport played on a diamond with four bases.

parts.note: a button that is pushed to ring for a servant or at a door

explanation.surface: Someone has been urged to pay a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressed' sounds like 'urged', but it is a button being pushed; 'call' is summoning by ringing.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorbell button is pushed to summon someone.

clue.text: Contented as Sir Mulberry Hawk was, perhaps

definitions.text: as Sir Mulberry Hawk was, perhaps
definitions.meaning: Sir Mulberry Hawk, a villain in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby, fights a duel, the gentleman's way of obtaining satisfaction

explanation.surface: A Dickens villain described as content.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Mulberry Hawk, the rake in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby, kills Lord Verisopht in a duel; a duel gave the challenger 'satisfaction' for an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Content means pleased; the other sense is having had honour avenged by a duel.

clue.text: Will perhaps include one TV man

indicators.note: to include is to hold inside, so the Bard takes the one in

parts.note: Will Shakespeare is called the Bard
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A last will may name a television presenter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' is not a legal document but Shakespeare, the Bard. John Logie Baird, a Scot, demonstrated television in 1926.
explanation.definitionFit: John Logie Baird was the Scottish engineer who pioneered television.

clue.text: Perhaps anchorages found on entering port

indicators.note: one word entering another goes inside it

parts.note: Lagos is a port, the chief harbour of Nigeria

explanation.surface: A harbour where boats anchor is found on reaching port.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example, hence 'Perhaps': lagoons can serve as sheltered anchorages.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheltered stretches of water cut off from the sea can serve ships as anchorages.

parts.note: US is the usual abbreviation for the United States
ages are long periods or eras of time

explanation.surface: Someone declares the periods during which customs duties apply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'States' looks like a verb meaning declares; it is the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Established practices and habits of a community are its customs.

clue.text: He looks on port, etc., as upsetting

indicators.note: upsetting means knocking over, so the letters of the words before are overturned into a new order

explanation.surface: A man watches as port and other drinks are knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' rearranges PORT ETC AS (nine letters).
explanation.definitionFit: An onlooker or watcher at an event is one who looks on.

definitions.meaning: as in 'it's all ... to me', meaning incomprehensible

explanation.surface: A complaint about incomprehensible speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incomprehensible is said to be 'all Greek'; it is also the tongue spoken in Athens.

parts.note: the phrase 'it goes without' this word means obviously; also a proverb is a set expression

explanation.surface: Something obvious needs no mention.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'it goes without ___' means 'obviously'; the answer fills the gap and also means a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom meaning plainly true lacks this word for an utterance or remark.

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of astonishment, as in 'Really?'

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned way of saying 'truly' that also shows surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are 'truly': the adverb of affirmation and the startled exclamation 'Really!'.

parts.note: a Lett is a member of the Baltic people of Latvia
gin is a spirit, a common crossword drink

explanation.surface: A Latvian guest is let in while holding a glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Allowing someone entry is a synonym phrase for admitting them.

parts.note: old slang calls the time of day 'the ...' ('How goes the ...?' asks the hour), and a foe is whom we hate

explanation.surface: A grumble about the passing hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How goes the enemy?' is an old phrase for 'What time is it?', because time is the foe of us all.
explanation.definitionFit: A foe or adversary is someone we hate, and old slang applies that word to time itself.

clue.text: Proper opener does badly — gets stumped ?

indicators.note: the opener of the word Proper is its first letter, a cricket term for a lead batsman
doing badly suggests a muddle, so the letters of 'does' are rearranged

explanation.surface: A proper opening batsman plays poorly and is stumped out at the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture (opener, stumped) is all surface: 'opener' takes the first letter and 'badly' is the anagram signal. 'Gets' only joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sense of the verb is to puzzle or perplex, so someone baffled by a question is stumped.

parts.note: in cricket a catch is 'taken' and six balls bowled make an 'over'; read normally, being caught up with by someone faster

explanation.surface: Two ways a cricket batsman can be dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled, and a catch is said to be taken; the whole word also means caught up and passed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being passed by a faster vehicle or person means being caught up with and left behind.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the two points sit on either side of the organ

parts.note: S, south, is a compass point, and two points give two of them
the liver is a bodily organ

explanation.surface: A music critic's remarks on pieces written for the organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests the musical instrument, but it is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Slivers are thin splinters or small fragments, so they are pieces of something.

parts.note: one has to be granted life, being, before anything else; the surface sounds like a gift you are owed

explanation.surface: Something you are owed or must receive.
explanation.walkthrough: Before you can be anything, you must be given being itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alive, simply being, is what anyone needs in order to be.

clue.text: Excessive fondness for female without attachment

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the female goes round the attachment

parts.note: a doe is a female deer or rabbit
a tag is a label attached to something

explanation.surface: Someone feels overly fond of a woman who has no romantic ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here has its old meaning of outside, not lacking, so it is a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Doting, an old sense of the word beside senility, means foolish or excessive affection.

clue.text: Statesman is pleased, with design for notes

parts.note: glad means pleased
is shortened to 's, as in 'he's'
tone is the quality or scheme of musical notes

explanation.surface: A politician is delighted with the new design for banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' gives S as in the contraction 's. William Gladstone was four times British Prime Minister in the 1800s.
explanation.definitionFit: William Gladstone was the Victorian Liberal Prime Minister.

clue.text: A blow for the farm worker

definitions.meaning: a labourer who turns and dries mown grass

explanation.surface: A setback for a farmhand.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer's wild swinging punch shares its name with the labourer who makes hay.

clue.text: Yearly letters in place of news

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, are the letters placed before a year's number
vice is the Latin preposition meaning in place of, as in vice-captain

explanation.surface: A notice of yearly correspondence sent instead of a newsletter.
explanation.walkthrough: AD (anno Domini) are the letters written with a year, and 'vice' is Latin for 'instead of'.
explanation.definitionFit: In older usage 'advices' were reports or tidings received from abroad, so the word meant news.

clue.text: See members about cover for leakage

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the letters go around the cover
the members, the letters, of the word See are rearranged

parts.note: a cap is a covering for the head or a bottle

explanation.surface: A bishop's see sends members to inspect a covering for a leak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' is an unusual anagram signal: the word's letters are its members, reordered, and 'about' wraps them round the cover. The surface's 'See' is a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: An escape of gas or water is a leak from where it should be held.

parts.note: a bar is a bolt for fastening a door
a second bar, since 'Bolts' is plural

explanation.surface: Someone runs off with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bolts' looks like a verb (runs away), but the plural noun gives two bars.
explanation.definitionFit: A common girl's name, so 'girl' stands for a woman bearing it.

parts.note: inspiration in its literal sense is drawing air into the lungs, rather than a creative idea

explanation.surface: Advice for a writer short of ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspiration literally means drawing in breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhaling air, the literal sense of inspiration, is what the lungs do.

clue.text: Has a taste for some craft?

definitions.meaning: tastes slightly of something, as in 'savours of'

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys handicrafts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' is boats, not handiwork; 'for' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Savours of something is one sense; sailing fishing boats are the other.

parts.note: a row of growing hair sitting above the mouth, the speaker; it pretends to be a growing quarrel about an orator

explanation.surface: A quarrel escalates about whoever is speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' is a line, not a quarrel, and the 'speaker' is the mouth beneath the upper lip.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial hair grown on the upper lip forms a line just above the mouth.

definitions.meaning: French for 'a bed', what a traveller asks for at an inn

explanation.surface: A gloomy Frenchman makes demands at a tavern.
explanation.walkthrough: Split in two, the answer is French for 'a bed', what a French traveller asks for at an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: Unilluminated means dark; the French words mean 'a bed'.

clue.text: A quondam petty cash total here?:

parts.note: d was the abbreviation for the old British penny, former small change
a sum is a total

explanation.surface: Someone asks where the old petty-cash total went.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British pence were written d (from Latin denarius), hence 'quondam' (former). The answer is the Latin roll-call reply.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin word, meaning 'I am present', is what a pupil answers at roll call.

parts.note: Thos is the short written form of the man's name Thomas

explanation.surface: A horse suitable for a small person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' looks like a horse; it is a mountain, the holy Mount in northern Greece. Thos is short for Thomas.
explanation.definitionFit: Athos is the Greek peninsula mountain famous for its monasteries.

parts.note: a punctuation stop of two dots, an intermediate break shorter than a full stop; surface is someone halting a pourer

explanation.surface: A drinker protests that the glass has only been half filled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' is a punctuation mark, not a command; old grammar ranked this mark as a stop weaker than the full stop.
explanation.definitionFit: This two-dot punctuation mark is a stop, ranked in old grammar below a full stop.

parts.note: a sewer is one who sews, and cobbling means rough mending; the surface suggests a shoemaker by a drain

explanation.surface: A shoemaker sets up shop beside a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' is someone who sews, not a drain, and 'cobbling' is patching together.
explanation.definitionFit: Needlework made of scraps stitched together is the mending a seamstress does.

definitions.meaning: a gundog breed, such as the Irish red one, which barks
the person who compiles a crossword

explanation.surface: A dog that turns out to compile crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a breed of gundog that barks; the other is the compiler of a crossword.

parts.note: split in two the answer says what irritated males do; a habit is also a garment, here clothing for males

explanation.surface: A bad habit that irritates others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' means clothing (as a nun's habit), and annoyed males are said to curse, which the answer read as two words says.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing for males is a habit in the garment sense, and cursing is a habit of irritated men.
